AfDB Doubles Angola's 2026 Growth Forecast to 5.8% as Mining and Lobito Corridor Investment Accelerate
text_paragraph_1: The African Development Bank has raised Angola's 2026 economic growth forecast from 2.9% to 5.8%, citing industrial investment, transport infrastructure and expanding activity in rare earth and other mining projects. Angola's economy grew 8.74% in the second quarter, supported by 16.46% mining growth and a 12.22% expansion in manufacturing. The $753 million Lobito railway financing package and the $250 million Longonjo rare earth project demonstrate growing investment beyond petroleum, although Longonjo remains under construction and is now targeting production in 2028. Oil continues to account for approximately 95% of export earnings and 60% of government revenue, leaving Angola exposed to international energy markets despite its improving economic outlook.
text_paragraph_2: Angola has received one of the largest economic growth upgrades in the African Development Bank's November 2026 outlook, with its forecast doubling from 2.9% to 5.8%. The revision follows stronger mining, manufacturing and transport activity, alongside investment in the Lobito Corridor and rare earth projects. Official statistics show GDP expanded 8.74% in the second quarter, with mining growing 16.46% and manufacturing 12.22%. However, oil still provides approximately 95% of export earnings, and several of the mineral projects supporting future growth have yet to begin commercial production.
text_paragraph_3: Angola's economic growth forecast for 2026 has doubled to 5.8%, from the 2.9% projected in May, as investment in mining, industrial production and transport infrastructure strengthens economic activity outside the country's historically dominant petroleum industry. The African Development Bank's November 13 Africa's Macroeconomic Performance and Outlook identifies Angola as the principal contributor to an improved Southern African growth forecast, reflecting increasing investment in rare earth minerals, other mining activities beyond diamonds and the logistics infrastructure intended to connect domestic mineral deposits with international markets.

For the past few months, Boris had spent most of his evenings at the café, one of thousands of invisible ‘microworkers’ in Africa who, for a pittance, help keep the wheels of the global AI industry turning.
text_paragraph_2: Boris performed one microtask after another on Remotasks, a platform run by Scale AI, a US company based in San Francisco and valued at $29bn in 2025. These involved locating, outlining and identifying objects in images to train AI systems to recognise them. Pictures of everyday life in the US and Europe scrolled across his screen. He identified pedestrians, cars and road signs, earning a few cents per task. ‘After four hours, I might have made the equivalent of 500 CFA francs,’ he said – less than $1.
text_paragraph_3: Like all the micro-workers I interviewed, Boris asked for his name to be changed, not because he is ashamed of doing work beneath his level of education, but out of fear of losing this meagre but valuable source of income in a country where 65% of the working population experiences some form of underemployment. Thousands of kilometres away, the data he annotates helps train the algorithms for self-driving cars and computer vision models in the global North.

text_paragraph_1: The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice has ordered the Guinea-Bissau government to pay 30 million CFA francs in compensation to five political figures over violations of their fundamental human rights. ‎ The court gave the ruling in Suit No. ECW/CCJ/APP/05/26, instituted in January by Nigerian law firm Adeola Oyinlade & Co, on behalf of the affected individualsfollowing their arbitrary detention by state authorities.
text_paragraph_2: The applicants are former Prime Minister of Guinea-Bissau and leader of the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), Domingos Simões Pereira; senior lawyer and PAIGC leader, Octávio Lopes; politician and Social Renewal Party (PRS) leader, Roberto Mbes’ba; PAIGC elected lawmaker, Marciano Indi and party lawyer and political commentator, Augusto Nansambe. ‎ The suit challenged their alleged arbitrary detention by Guinea-Bissau authorities, with the applicants seeking redress for violations of their fundamental rights. ‎ Nansambe was reportedly assaulted and abducted from his residence by armed men on December 28, 2025, amid political tensions in the West African country. ‎ The law firm, led by its Senior Partner and Lead Counsel, Adeola Austin Oyinlade, described the judgment as an affirmation of the rights to personal liberty, human dignity and effective judicial protection under regional and international human rights law. ‎ Oyinlade said the case was not limited to the political standing of any of the applicants but concerned the protection of fundamental freedoms across West Africa. ‎ “This case has never been merely about one individual. From the outset, we made clear that it was about safeguarding the dignity and fundamental freedoms of all citizens across West Africa”, he said. ‎ Oyinlade urged the Guinea-Bissau government to comply with the judgment, warning that the recognition of rights by a court would be meaningless without practical enforcement. ‎ “We now expect fullcompliance with the judgment. A judicial ruling protecting personal liberty must not remain a mere declaration on paper. Justice is complete only when the rights recognised by the Court are effectively enjoyed by those to whom they belong.” ‎ The judgment was coming amid international concerns over political detentions and the restoration of constitutional order in Guinea-Bissau following the November 2025 political crisis. ‎ African Union Peace and Security Council had repeatedly called for the immediate and unconditional release of Pereira and other political detainees, urging respect for fundamental freedoms. ‎ The United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights had also expressed concern over arbitrary arrests and detentions following the political crisis, calling for the release of persons held without due legal process.
text_paragraph_3: ‎Reacting to the ruling, Oyinlade described it as a significant development for the applicants, their families and advocates of the rule of law.

title: Benin: the return of Sèmè oil and the broadening of partnerships
text_paragraph_1: In Benin, recent developments highlight the new levers on which Cotonou intends to build its ambitions. After nearly three decades of interruption, Beninese oil is returning to international trade channels with the resumption of production at the offshore Sèmè field and the loading of a first cargo of 330,000 barrels. This revival opens up new revenue prospects, but raises the question of the State's capacity to sustainably manage the development of this resource. At the same time, Benin is seeking to diversify its partnerships: at the Russia-Africa summit in Moscow, it set out its priorities in agriculture, energy and local processing, while the prospect of a military cooperation agreement with Russia has been raised. Finally, on the security front, the review of the Coastal States Stability Mechanism shows that the prevention of violent extremism in the north of the country increasingly relies on community anchoring and local ownership.
text_paragraph_2: After nearly three decades of interruption, Beninese oil is about to return to international trade channels. The resumption of production at the offshore Sèmè field , long uncertain, is now under way, as Cotonou seeks to strengthen its economic capacities and diversify its sources of partnership. Nevertheless, the question remains of the country's ability to convert its natural resources into genuine levers of development, insofar as, between operating conditions, revenue management and prospects for transforming its economy, the return of Beninese crude opens up as many opportunities as it raises challenges.
text_paragraph_3: In this context, the return of Sèmè oil opens up a new economic prospect for Cotonou, while raising the question of the conditions under which this resource can contribute sustainably to the country's ambitions. A first cargo of around 330,000 barrels of crude is due to be loaded on 1 and 2 November 2026 aboard the tanker Kriti Jade, bound for the Netherlands. This shipment marks an important milestone for the offshore Sèmè field, discovered in 1967 and operated between 1982 and 1998, a period during which some 22 million barrels were extracted. Several attempts to revive the field had so far failed to durably restore commercial production. The new start of operations therefore opens an unprecedented chapter for Benin's oil sector, even though its economic scale remains to be assessed in light of production and marketing conditions.

text_paragraph_2: En quelques semaines, l’océan Indien a vu se succéder des crises sociales d’une intensité rare. Il y a un an, Madagascar était secoué par un soulèvement de jeunes, parti des coupures d’eau et d’électricité, qui a chassé le président Rajoelina du pouvoir. Début octobre, la presse régionale relevait des fragilités communes, du coût de la vie à La Réunion aux tensions budgétaires à Mayotte. C’est désormais Maurice, habituellement cité comme un modèle de stabilité et de prospérité africaine, qui traverse des émeutes d’une ampleur inédite depuis 1999 selon les observateurs, dont l’historien et politologue mauricien Jocelyn Chan Low. text_paragraph_3: Ancienne colonie sucrière devenue indépendante en 1968, Maurice a bâti sa prospérité sur une diversification réussie, du textile au tourisme et à la finance internationale, qui la place parmi les économies africaines aux revenus les plus élevés, dépendance aux importations incluses. Ce parcours masque les fragilités croissantes. Entre dette publique élevée et vie politique dominée depuis des décennies par les mêmes formations, dont celle de Navin Ramgoolamn Premier ministre, de retour au pouvoir depuis novembre 2024, avec l’Alliance du Changement, élu sur une promesse de justice sociale attendue impatiemment par la population mauricienne.

South Africa’s ANC Is Collapsing. The Far Right Is Rising.
text_paragraph_1: W hile the global left celebrates the recent successes of the Workers’ Party in Brazil and the Democratic Socialists of America in the United States, the African National Congress (ANC) has suffered a historic collapse in South Africa’s November 4 local government elections. After three decades of mass unemployment, deepening inequality, corruption, and economic policies that have failed the working class, the former liberation movement is losing its political authority. The principal beneficiaries of the ANC’s electoral rout are parties of the Right, including an increasingly powerful far right that has built its project around aggressive and often violent xenophobia.
text_paragraph_2: With more than 70 percent of votes counted, the ANC’s national share of the vote fell to around 32 percent. The ANC is not expected to retain an outright majority in any major city, and the center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), historically the principal party of the white liberal establishment, is making substantial gains and is projected to become the largest party in most of South Africa’s big cities. Former President Jacob Zuma’s Zulu nationalist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) is on track to be the largest party in Durban. The far-right ActionSA has made a strong showing in Johannesburg and Pretoria and is likely to be the second-largest party in Pretoria, with the ANC in third place.
text_paragraph_3: The central question is not only why the ANC has lost so much support. It is why the suffering and anger of the working class have failed to produce a powerful democratic socialist alternative, and why the Right has been so successful in presenting itself as the answer to a crisis created by the existing economic and political order.

Shelter Afrique sustainable bond backs affordable housing in West Africa
text_paragraph_1: The pan-African development bank's inaugural FCFA 60 billion sustainable bond will finance more than 17,500 affordable and energy-efficient homes across the WAEMU region.
text_paragraph_2: Shelter Afrique Development Bank (ShafDB) has successfully closed its inaugural FCFA 60 billion sustainable bond, raising approximately $100 million to finance affordable and sustainable housing projects across member countries of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU). The bond, the first sustainable issuance by the pan-African development finance institution in the regional market, attracted strong demand from a broad mix of investors during the subscription period from 7 to 30 October 2026. The transaction comprises a five-year tranche offering a 6.10% return and a seven-year tranche at 6.30%. CGF Bourse served as lead arranger, while UCA acted as co-lead manager. The International Finance Corporation (IFC) and Ecobank Group, through Ecobank Senegal, participated as anchor investors, with the West African Development Bank (BOAD) among the key financial partners. ShafDB said the proceeds will be used exclusively to finance affordable, sustainable and energy-efficient housing projects across the WAEMU region, helping address a significant housing shortfall while promoting environmentally responsible urban development. According to estimates cited by the World Bank Group, the WAEMU region faces a housing deficit of approximately 3.5 million units, with demand growing by nearly 250,000 homes annually. The first phase of the financing programme is expected to support a pipeline of 17,554 housing units and create an estimated 87,772 jobs across the region. Speaking after signing an agreement for IFC's anchor investment on the sidelines of the 2026 African Financial Summit (AFIS) in Angola, IFC Managing Director Makhtar Diop said Africa possessed substantial domestic savings that could be channelled towards addressing the continent's housing challenges. “Africa has the capital to finance more of its own housing needs. The opportunity is to connect those savings with long-term investment that can put more families in homes, strengthen local businesses and create jobs,” Diop said. He described the partnership with ShafDB as an important step towards developing deeper local capital markets capable of financing housing development across the continent. Ecobank Group Chief Executive Officer Jeremy Awori said the transaction demonstrated the benefits of regional collaboration in addressing housing needs and supporting the broader housing value chain. ShafDB Managing Director Thierno-Habib Hann said the successful issuance illustrated how African and international institutions could work together to mobilise long-term domestic capital for housing development. “With a housing deficit of over 53 million units, no single institution can close this gap alone,” Hann said. “That is why we structured this transaction with commercial, regional and international partners to accelerate access to affordable, sustainable housing and invest in the broader housing value chain.” He added that the partnership with IFC, Ecobank, BOAD and other stakeholders provides a model that could be replicated in other African markets. A key feature of the local-currency bond is that it aligns financing with project revenues, reducing borrowers' exposure to foreign-exchange risk while supporting the growth of regional capital markets.

text_paragraph_1: The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice has ordered the Guinea-Bissau government to pay 30 million CFA francs in compensation to five political figures over violations of their fundamental human rights. ‎ The court gave the ruling in Suit No. ECW/CCJ/APP/05/26, instituted in January by Nigerian law firm Adeola Oyinlade & Co, on behalf of the affected individualsfollowing their arbitrary detention by state authorities.
text_paragraph_2: The applicants are former Prime Minister of Guinea-Bissau and leader of the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), Domingos Simões Pereira; senior lawyer and PAIGC leader, Octávio Lopes; politician and Social Renewal Party (PRS) leader, Roberto Mbes’ba; PAIGC elected lawmaker, Marciano Indi and party lawyer and political commentator, Augusto Nansambe. ‎ The suit challenged their alleged arbitrary detention by Guinea-Bissau authorities, with the applicants seeking redress for violations of their fundamental rights. ‎ Nansambe was reportedly assaulted and abducted from his residence by armed men on December 28, 2025, amid political tensions in the West African country. ‎ The law firm, led by its Senior Partner and Lead Counsel, Adeola Austin Oyinlade, described the judgment as an affirmation of the rights to personal liberty, human dignity and effective judicial protection under regional and international human rights law. ‎ Oyinlade said the case was not limited to the political standing of any of the applicants but concerned the protection of fundamental freedoms across West Africa. ‎ “This case has never been merely about one individual. From the outset, we made clear that it was about safeguarding the dignity and fundamental freedoms of all citizens across West Africa”, he said. ‎ Oyinlade urged the Guinea-Bissau government to comply with the judgment, warning that the recognition of rights by a court would be meaningless without practical enforcement. ‎ “We now expect fullcompliance with the judgment. A judicial ruling protecting personal liberty must not remain a mere declaration on paper. Senegal: from a budget of discord to a political “divorce” now final
text_paragraph_1: In Senegal, the split between President Bassirou Diomaye Faye and Ousmane Sonko is now openly acknowledged. On Saturday 14 November, before party officials gathered in Dakar, the Speaker of the National Assembly and leader of Pastef declared: “Politically, the divorce is complete, once and for all.” This statement crowns several weeks of confrontation between the executive and the legislature. On 3 November, the Assembly rejected the 2026 amended budget law. Since 7 November, its finance committee has been rejecting most of the 2027 budget bills, citing a lack of credibility in the forecasts. The budget standoff, against the backdrop of negotiations with the IMF, is thus taking an openly political turn. As the dissolution of the Assembly becomes constitutionally possible and local elections draw closer, the country is entering a period of strong polarisation.
text_paragraph_2: The tug-of-war has probably never been so visible. In the space of a few days, the National Assembly delivered three successive rejections of the amended budget bill (LFR) for 2026. An unusual episode in Senegalese parliamentary life in recent years, this triple rebuff sharply reveals the depth of the duel now being played out between the executive and legislative branches, against the backdrop of a rift between the camps of Ousmane Sonko and Diomaye Faye. Indeed, the rejection, on 3 November, of the 2026 LFR bill by the National Assembly puts the executive in a delicate position, as Senegal seeks to consolidate its agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Only a few days earlier, on 27 October, the text had been sent back to the technical committee at the government's request, as it still hoped to reach a compromise with the parliamentary majority. This was before the text was officially rejected three days later. If proof were still needed, these episodes demonstrate the intransigence of the Pastef parliamentary majority in its determination to act as a counterweight to the executive.
text_paragraph_3: At the heart of the disagreement lie the transparency of budgetary trade-offs, the preservation of public investment and guarantees on purchasing power. Ousmane Sonko's party notably contests the proposed cuts in appropriations for health, education, water and infrastructure, arguing that savings should instead focus on non-priority operating expenditure. The parliamentary majority also says it is concerned about the weight of energy subsidies, whose 2026 forecasts have changed significantly compared with initial estimates. For Pastef, any reduction in these subsidies should be accompanied by measures to ease taxation on petroleum products and electricity supply costs. These are reservations that the government's explanations have clearly failed to dispel. Defending the text, Prime Minister Ahmadou Al Aminou Lô had tried to point out, at a press conference on 25 October, that this budget revision was a response to falling public revenue and rising expenditure, particularly due to higher energy prices. The head of government also stressed that the bill was an extension of the initial budget law drawn up when Ousmane Sonko was still leading the government. But to no avail.

title: Shelter Afrique sustainable bond backs affordable housing in West Africa
text_paragraph_1: The pan-African development bank's inaugural FCFA 60 billion sustainable bond will finance more than 17,500 affordable and energy-efficient homes across the WAEMU region.
text_paragraph_2: Shelter Afrique Development Bank (ShafDB) has successfully closed its inaugural FCFA 60 billion sustainable bond, raising approximately $100 million to finance affordable and sustainable housing projects across member countries of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (WAEMU). The bond, the first sustainable issuance by the pan-African development finance institution in the regional market, attracted strong demand from a broad mix of investors during the subscription period from 7 to 30 October 2026. The transaction comprises a five-year tranche offering a 6.10% return and a seven-year tranche at 6.30%. CGF Bourse served as lead arranger, while UCA acted as co-lead manager. The International Finance Corporation (IFC) and Ecobank Group, through Ecobank Senegal, participated as anchor investors, with the West African Development Bank (BOAD) among the key financial partners. ShafDB said the proceeds will be used exclusively to finance affordable, sustainable and energy-efficient housing projects across the WAEMU region, helping address a significant housing shortfall while promoting environmentally responsible urban development. According to estimates cited by the World Bank Group, the WAEMU region faces a housing deficit of approximately 3.5 million units, with demand growing by nearly 250,000 homes annually. The first phase of the financing programme is expected to support a pipeline of 17,554 housing units and create an estimated 87,772 jobs across the region. He described the partnership with ShafDB as an important step towards developing deeper local capital markets capable of financing housing development across the continent. Ecobank Group Chief Executive Officer Jeremy Awori said the transaction demonstrated the benefits of regional collaboration in addressing housing needs and supporting the broader housing value chain. ShafDB Managing Director Thierno-Habib Hann said the successful issuance illustrated how African and international institutions could work together to mobilise long-term domestic capital for housing development. “With a housing deficit of over 53 million units, no single institution can close this gap alone,” Hann said. “That is why we structured this transaction with commercial, regional and international partners to accelerate access to affordable, sustainable housing and invest in the broader housing value chain.” He added that the partnership with IFC, Ecobank, BOAD and other stakeholders provides a model that could be replicated in other African markets. title: Bundibugyo ebolavirus: A wake-up call for pandemic preparedness
text_paragraph_1: The 2026 outbreak of Bundibugyo virus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has turned a relatively neglected Ebola virus into a major international public health concern. First identified in 2007 in the Bundibugyo district of western Uganda, Bundibugyo virus is a distinct species of Orthoebolavirus and has previously caused only two recognized outbreaks. Its limited history has meant comparatively little investment in diagnostics, vaccines, therapeutics and epidemic preparedness. (1)
text_paragraph_2: The present outbreak, however, is different in scale. It began in Ituri Province of DRC in April 2026 and subsequently spread across multiple provinces and across the border into Uganda. The World Health Organization declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on May 17, 2026. As of Sept. 13, 2026, DRC had reported 7,258 confirmed cases and 3,510 deaths, with a case-fatality ratio of 48.4%. The outbreak had expanded to 62 health zones in seven provinces, including the newly affected South Ubangi Province. (2) By Oct. 15, 2026, the outbreak spread to the North Ubangi Province, bordering the Central African Republic, making it the eighth province to be affected. (3)
text_paragraph_3: By early October, total cases reached 8,300 and 4,018 deaths, including 50 health workers, of which one was evacuated to the Netherlands. (4) A Kenyan man died in Nairobi on Oct. 5, 2026, after returning from DRC. This was the first death from Kenya. Meanwhile, on Oct. 20, 2026, the first Ebola case was reported from Nigeria in its capital, Abuja. This was a Swiss woman who had arrived from Uganda. (5) After improvement, she was medically evacuated to Switzerland on Oct. 27, 2026. (6)

Power relations and agency in Somalia’s election process
text_paragraph_1: Somalia’s electoral history has been marked by significant shifts since independence. After gaining independence in 1960, the country held elections based on universal suffrage, including local elections in 1963 and parliamentary elections in 1964 and 1969 (Samatar 2015). This democratic period came to an end following the military coup led by Mohamed Siad Barre in 1969, which ushered in an authoritarian regime that lasted until the collapse of the state in 1991. Since then, Somalia has yet to hold a national election based on universal suffrage.
text_paragraph_2: The debate over elections in Somalia reflects a longstanding difference in approach. The international community (IC) has often advocated for universal suffrage, while Somali political actors have frequently relied on clan-based electoral arrangements. They argue that electoral systems need to take account of local political realities, historical experiences, and established ways of managing conflict. These differences are about more than voting procedures or institutional design. At their heart are deeper questions about who holds political authority, whose vision of legitimacy prevails, and how sovereignty, partnership, ownership, power, and agency are negotiated within Somalia’s state-building process.
text_paragraph_3: Clan-based electoral arrangements, therefore, should not be viewed simply as evidence of institutional weakness or democratic failure. They are rooted in a longer history of political organisation that predates colonial rule and the modern state (Lewis 1961). Following the collapse of the Somali state in 1991, and amid the absence of strong national institutions and a robust constitutional framework, clan structures also helped maintain social order, resolve disputes, and facilitate political negotiations (Gundel 2006). For many Somali political actors, these arrangements are consequently more than a temporary compromise. They remain a practical and, in some contexts, legitimate way of managing political competition in a fragmented political landscape.

text_paragraph_1: B oris L was working late into the evening in the gloom of a cramped, dusty Internet café in the Ngoa Ékélé district of Cameroon’s capital, his face bathed in the blue glow from a second-hand screen. Outside, Yaoundé’s university district had been plunged into darkness by yet another of the power cuts for which Cameroon’s electricity company, Socadel, is notorious. But here, an old generator rumbled away in the back room and the Internet connection held up. For the past few months, Boris had spent most of his evenings at the café, one of thousands of invisible ‘microworkers’ in Africa who, for a pittance, help keep the wheels of the global AI industry turning.
text_paragraph_2: Boris performed one microtask after another on Remotasks, a platform run by Scale AI, a US company based in San Francisco and valued at $29bn in 2025. These involved locating, outlining and identifying objects in images to train AI systems to recognise them. Pictures of everyday life in the US and Europe scrolled across his screen. He identified pedestrians, cars and road signs, earning a few cents per task. ‘After four hours, I might have made the equivalent of 500 CFA francs,’ he said – less than $1.
text_paragraph_3: Like all the micro-workers I interviewed, Boris asked for his name to be changed, not because he is ashamed of doing work beneath his level of education, but out of fear of losing this meagre but valuable source of income in a country where 65% of the working population experiences some form of underemployment. Thousands of kilometres away, the data he annotates helps train the algorithms for self-driving cars and computer vision models in the global North.
